{{short description|American mathematician and physicist}}
'''Hubert Lewis Bray''' is an American mathematician. A [[differential geometry|differential geometer]], he is known for proving the [[Riemannian Penrose inequality]] in 1999.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Riemannian Penrose inequality and a virtual gravitational collapse|journal = Physical Review D|date = 2009-08-13|article-number = 047501|volume = 80|issue = 4|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.80.047501|first1 = Seiju|last1 = Ohashi|first2 = Tetsuya|last2 = Shiromizu|first3 = Sumio|last3 = Yamada|arxiv=0906.2042|bibcode = 2009PhRvD..80d7501O|s2cid = 55991838}}</ref> He works as professor of mathematics and physics at [[Duke University]], specializing in differential geometry.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Fine-tuning Stephen Hawking's theory of mass|url = http://phys.org/news/2014-03-fine-tuning-stephen-hawking-theory-mass.html|access-date = 2015-08-05}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
In 1988, after placing 4th in the USA Math Olympiad, Bray achieved a bronze medal in the International Math Olympiad. In 1991, as an undergraduate student at Rice University, he was awarded the Hubert Evelyn Bray Prize in Mathematics, named after his grandfather, who was the first PhD recipient of Rice Institute. He earned his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] and [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degrees in [[Mathematics]] and [[Physics]] in 1992 from [[Rice University]] and obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1997 from [[Stanford University]] under the mentorship of [[Richard Melvin Schoen]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = The Mathematics Genealogy Project - Hubert Bray|url = http://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=39251|website = www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|access-date = 2015-08-05}}</ref>

== Career ==
He was an invited speaker at the 2002 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Beijing]] (in the section of [[differential geometry]]).<ref>[http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171124141541/http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php |date=2017-11-24 }} ([[International Mathematical Union]])</ref>

He is one of the inaugural fellows of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows] of the [[American Mathematical Society]]</ref>

Hubert was appointed professor of mathematics in 2004, an additionally professor of physics in 2019. In 2019, he was appointed director of undergraduate studies of Duke's mathematics department.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholars.duke.edu/person/hubert.bray|title=Hubert Bray {{!}} Scholars@Duke|last=|first=|date=|website=Duke University|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Hubert is the grandson of Hubert Evelyn Bray, professor of mathematics at [[Rice University]] and the first person awarded a Ph.D. by the then [[Rice Institute]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Photographers|first=Stan Begam's The Bel-Air Co|date=1962|title=Hubert Bray, Rice University|url=https://scholarship.rice.edu/handle/1911/75752|journal=Rice University Archives General Photo Files, "Individuals - Bray, Hunert Evelyn," Woodson Research Center, Fondren Library, Rice University|hdl=1911/75752|language=en}}</ref>

Hubert Bray and his brother [[Clark Bray]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.duke.edu/people/clark-bray|title=Clark Bray {{!}} Department of Mathematics|website=math.duke.edu|access-date=2019-10-31}}</ref> share similar educations and jobs, both having studied at [[Rice University]] (undergraduate),<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3U7tresTD1AC&q=hubert+bray+clark+bray&pg=PP1|title=Lebesgue Integration on Euclidean Space|last=Jones|first=Frank|date=2001|publisher=Jones & Bartlett Learning|isbn=978-0-7637-1708-7|language=en}}</ref> [[Stanford University]] (graduate), and are professors of mathematics at [[Duke University]].
